content.overview: Dryback describes the reduction in root-zone water content between defined measurement points. Its magnitude and rate should be interpreted with media, crop stage, environment, irrigation history and sensor method rather than as a universal percentage or elapsed-time rule.

vocabulary.definition: Reduction in measured root-zone water content between defined times or events.
Change in measured water content per unit time over a defined interval.
The sequence and shape of root-zone measurements over time rather than one isolated value.

sections.title: Calculate from comparable measurements
sections.body: Use consistent sensor placement, units and timing. A change from 70% to 46% water content is a 24-percentage-point dryback, but that number has meaning only in the stated system and interval.

sections.title: Rate can matter as much as magnitude
sections.body: The same total dryback reached rapidly or slowly can reflect different crop demand, environmental load or irrigation timing.

sections.title: Do not universalize a steering number
sections.body: Media properties, container size, cultivar, stage, root mass and environment alter the relationship between dryback and plant response. Use facility-validated ranges and measured response rather than copied percentages.

workedExamples: A 20-point dryback over four hours under intense light is not equivalent evidence to the same change over fourteen hours in a different media and environment.
commonMistakes: Using clock time alone as dryback.
Copying one dryback percentage across all media.
Ignoring irrigation event size and sensor location.
content.practicalApplication: Graph a mock dryback curve and identify irrigation events, fastest depletion intervals and evidence needed before changing a steering target.
content.summary: Dryback is a context-dependent trajectory that should be measured, trended and interpreted—not memorized as a universal percentage.
